key_terms.meaning: Study matter through bulk measurable quantities such as p, V, T; no molecule-by-molecule tracking (classical thermodynamics).
Study matter through the behaviour of individual molecules and their statistics (statistical thermodynamics, kinetic theory).
The fixed quantity of matter or the fixed region in space that we choose to study.
The real or imaginary surface that separates the system from its surroundings and across which mass and energy may pass.
A system with fixed mass; energy may cross the boundary but no mass does.
A chosen region in space across whose boundary both mass and energy can flow.
A system in which neither mass nor energy crosses the boundary; Q = 0 and W = 0.
A wall that does not allow heat transfer; a rigid and insulated wall is both adiabatic and fixed.
A wall that allows heat to pass, so two bodies on either side can reach the same temperature.
Condition in which properties at a fixed point do not change with time, though mass still flows through (open system).
A measurable characteristic of the system, such as p, V, T, or density; a state is fixed when enough properties are fixed.
A property independent of mass, e.g. pressure p (Pa), temperature T (K), density ρ (kg/m³).
A property that depends on the size of the system, e.g. volume V (m³), mass m (kg), total energy E (J).
An extensive property divided by mass, e.g. v = V/m (m³/kg), u = U/m (J/kg).
A state is the complete condition of the system at one instant; the sequence of states passed through is the path.
A process is a change from state 1 to state 2; a cycle is a process (or series of processes) that returns to the starting state.
No unbalanced driving force inside the system or across its boundary: mechanical, thermal and chemical equilibrium all hold.
A process in which every intermediate state is infinitesimally close to equilibrium, so properties are defined throughout the path.
If A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with B; temperature is the property they share.
A property that changes measurably and repeatably with temperature, e.g. length of mercury, pressure of a gas at constant volume, resistance.
Energy crossing the boundary because of an intensive driving force acting through a displacement; unit joule (J), sign positive when done by the system.
Energy crossing the boundary only because of a temperature difference; unit joule (J), sign positive when added to the system.
Work done by expansion against pressure: W = ∫p dV, equal to the area under the p–V path; unit J.

takeaways: Thermodynamics can be built either from molecular behaviour (microscopic) or from bulk measurable properties (macroscopic); engineering uses the macroscopic route.
The boundary you draw decides everything: whether mass crosses makes the system closed or open, whether heat crosses makes the wall diathermic or adiabatic.
Intensive properties are size-independent, extensive ones scale with mass, and specific properties are extensive properties per kilogram.
A state is a snapshot, fixed by enough properties; a path through states is a process, and a closed path is a cycle.
Equilibrium means no unbalanced force, temperature difference or chemical tendency; only near-equilibrium states can be treated with simple property relations.
A quasi-static process is an idealised slow process through near-equilibrium states, which is why p–V work can be integrated as ∫p dV.
The zeroth law is what makes temperature a measurable, comparable quantity rather than a personal feeling.
Every thermometer works by assuming one thermometric property varies linearly enough with temperature; each scale differs only in the fixed points and the property chosen.
Work and heat are energy in transit across a boundary, not stored properties, so they depend on the path and their signs must be fixed before any calculation.
Displacement work W = ∫p dV is only the most common work mode; shaft, spring, elastic, electric, magnetic and surface-tension work all follow force × displacement.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually built around a definition-plus-classification question followed by a diagram and a short numerical or derivation, so keep clean p–V sketches, correct signs and stated units ready.

bank.q: Define system, boundary and surroundings. Classify thermodynamic systems into closed, open and isolated, and give one engineering example of each with a sketch showing mass and energy crossing.
outline: Clear definitions of the three terms
Closed: fixed mass, energy may cross (piston-cylinder, sealed cooker)
Open: control volume, mass and energy cross (boiler feed pump, turbine, human body)
Isolated: neither mass nor energy (perfect vacuum flask, ideal calorimeter)
Sketches with boundary drawn as a dashed line and arrows for mass/energy

bank.q: Distinguish between intensive and extensive properties, and between specific and total properties. Show that density is intensive while volume is extensive.
outline: Definition of intensive: independent of mass
Definition of extensive: proportional to mass
Specific property = extensive/mass
Halving the system halves V but leaves p and T unchanged
Examples with units: p (Pa), T (K), V (m³), v (m³/kg)

bank.q: Define state, state point, path, process and cycle. Explain how many independent properties are needed to fix a state of a simple compressible system.
outline: State as a complete condition described by properties
State point on a p–V or T–v diagram
Process as a path between two states
Cycle returns to the initial state, net property change zero
Two independent intensive properties fix a simple compressible state (state postulate)
Quasi-static restriction for drawing a continuous path

bank.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it leads to the idea of temperature and to the use of a thermometer.
outline: Exact statement with three systems A, B, C
Transitivity of thermal equilibrium
Temperature as the property common to systems in equilibrium
Thermometer as system C brought into contact and read
Need for a thermometric property and fixed points

bank.q: Compare the microscopic and macroscopic approaches to thermodynamics. State the merits and limitations of each and say which one engineering calculations use.
outline: Microscopic: molecular positions, velocities, statistics, large number of variables
Macroscopic: few bulk variables such as p, V, T, no molecular detail
Microscopic gives physical insight (internal energy origin), macroscopic gives easy measurement
Macroscopic cannot explain why Cp > Cv without microscopic help
Engineering design calculations use the macroscopic approach

bank.q: A gas expands in a piston-cylinder from V₁ = 0.10 m³ to V₂ = 0.30 m³. Evaluate the displacement work if the path is (a) constant pressure p = 200 kPa, and (b) pV = constant with p₁ = 200 kPa. Comment on the two answers.
outline: W = ∫p dV for each path
(b) W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 20 000 × ln 3 ≈ 22 kJ
Same end states, different work: work is a path function
Units carried throughout

bank.q: A gas in a cylinder is compressed with 40 kJ of work input while 25 kJ of heat leaves it to the surroundings. Fix a sign convention, write down the values of W and Q with signs, and state the net energy change of the gas.
outline: Convention stated: Q positive into system, W positive by system
W = −40 kJ, Q = −25 kJ
Energy balance ΔE = Q − W = −25 + 40 = +15 kJ
Physical meaning: internal energy rises by 15 kJ
Warning that reversing the convention flips both signs but not the physics

bank.q: Write the expressions for work done in stretching an elastic rod, in blowing a soap bubble against surface tension, and in charging a capacitor or moving a charge through a potential difference. Explain the force × displacement pattern in each.
outline: Generalised work δW = F dx or Y dX
Elastic: δW = −σ dA or F dL with tension and length change
Surface tension: δW = σ dA, dA for a bubble film (two surfaces)
Electrical: δW = V dq or E di dt
Identify the intensive property (force, surface tension, potential) and the conjugate displacement

bank.q: Two bodies at 300 K and 400 K are separated first by a diathermic wall and then by an adiabatic wall. Describe what happens in each case, name the process in the diathermic case for the hotter body, and state the final condition.
outline: Diathermic: heat flows from 400 K body to 300 K body until temperatures are equal
Final temperature between 300 K and 400 K, value from energy balance
Thermal equilibrium reached, zeroth law applies
Adiabatic: no heat flow, temperatures stay different
Adiabatic wall makes the two parts separate systems

bank.q: A constant-volume gas thermometer reads a pressure of 100.0 kPa at the ice point and 136.6 kPa at the steam point. Find the temperature when the pressure is 118.0 kPa, assuming p varies linearly with T. State the thermometric property used.
outline: Linear relation T = 273.15 (p/p_ice) or the two-point form
Thermometric property = pressure of fixed mass of gas at constant volume
Comment on ideal-gas temperature scale and why real gas readings need correction

bank.q: Using p–V diagrams, show that work and heat are path functions while pressure, volume and temperature are point functions. Explain why a cycle returns zero net change of properties but not necessarily zero net work or heat.
outline: Two different paths between the same states give different areas and hence different W
Properties depend only on the state, so ∮dp = ∮dV = ∮dT = 0
∮δW = net area enclosed by the cycle, generally not zero
∮δQ = ∮δW for a cycle
Use of exact versus inexact differential notation
Statement that heat and work exist only during a process

bank.q: Assess why the zeroth law is stated as a law at all. Discuss what would fail in thermometry without transitivity of thermal equilibrium, and comment on the practical limits of a real thermometer.
outline: Law gives transitivity of 'is in equilibrium with'
Without it a temperature scale cannot be assigned consistently
Empirical temperature defined by a chosen thermometric property
Different thermometers agree only for ideal-gas scale; real gases deviate
Limits: finite thermometer disturbs the system, finite response time, limited range
Constant-volume gas thermometer as the practical standard

bank.q: Contrast a quasi-static process with a real rapid process in an engine cylinder. Evaluate the error made in using W = ∫p dV for the real process, and state when the quasi-static assumption is acceptable.
outline: Quasi-static: infinite slowness, uniform properties, well-defined path
Real process: pressure gradients, turbulence, non-equilibrium states
W = ∫p dV uses the system pressure p, valid only if p is uniform
For rapid expansion against a known external pressure, use W = ∫p_ext dV
Error grows with speed of the process and with pressure non-uniformity
Acceptable when process time is much larger than relaxation time; uniform-property assumption stated explicitly

bank.q: Distinguish thermodynamic equilibrium from steady state using an open-system example such as a steam turbine or a running pump. Explain why a steady-flow device can be analysed with equilibrium property tables.
outline: Equilibrium: no change with time and no unbalanced driving force within the system
Steady state: properties at each point constant in time, but gradients and flow exist
Turbine inlet and outlet states steady while the flow is not in equilibrium internally
Local equilibrium assumption permits property tables at inlet and outlet
State the three parts of equilibrium: mechanical, thermal, chemical
Consequence: energy balance can be written between inlet and outlet only

glossary.def: The science of energy, its forms, its transformations, and the direction in which transformations can occur.
The fixed mass or fixed region chosen for study, separated from everything else by a boundary.
Everything outside the boundary of the system that can interact with it.
The surface, real or imaginary, that encloses the system and across which interactions are counted.
A fixed region in space with an open boundary through which mass and energy flow; the basis of open-system analysis.
A characteristic of the system that can be measured or calculated, such as pressure, volume or temperature.
A property whose value does not change when the system is divided, e.g. pressure or temperature.
A property that is proportional to the amount of matter, e.g. mass, volume, total energy.
The complete condition of a system described by its properties at one instant.
A change of state, that is, the path taken from one equilibrium state to another.
The series of intermediate states passed through during a process.
A process or set of processes that returns the system to its initial state.
The condition in which mechanical, thermal and chemical driving forces are all balanced, so no change occurs with time.
An idealised infinitely slow process in which every intermediate state is essentially in equilibrium.
A condition in which properties at every fixed point stay constant with time while mass continues to flow.
Two systems each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in thermal equilibrium with each other, which makes temperature a valid property.
Any property that changes in a known, repeatable way with temperature and is used to build a thermometer.
The property that is equal for systems in thermal equilibrium; it decides the direction of heat flow.
Energy transferred across a boundary solely because of a temperature difference, measured in joules.
Energy transferred across a boundary by an intensive force acting through a displacement, measured in joules.
Work done as a system's volume changes against pressure, given by W = ∫p dV.
A quantity whose change depends only on the end states, like a property; examples are p, V, T, U.
A quantity whose value depends on the route taken between states, like heat and work.
A boundary that permits heat transfer, allowing two bodies to reach the same temperature.
A boundary that prevents heat transfer completely.
A temperature value assigned by a chosen thermometer and scale, valid through the thermometric property it uses.
